title: Query
meta: Browse data and save read-only SQL
intro: Use Query to browse enabled database connectors, inspect workflow datasets and save SELECT statements as Custom Queries. Report Designer can bind tables to those saved queries.

Start with your own connector and received data. No documentation sample data is required. The count example below also returns a useful result when the warehouse is empty. The pictures use a separate test installation.

You need Use query workbench. Queries read data. Statements that change data or tables are refused. A new installation creates a target-warehouse connector for its configured database engine. These pictures use Target Warehouse (Postgres). Other sources need a matching enabled database connector.
Saved built-in queries can supply reports. Inspect them freely, but understand those report dependencies before changing SQL or parameter identifiers.

tasks.title: Browse a source table
intro: Use this to inspect a connector schema before writing SQL. A schema is the database namespace containing its tables.
steps: Select Query in the main menu.
Select the enabled database connector. The example uses Target Warehouse (Postgres).
Select the schema, such as public for the PostgreSQL warehouse.
Select the table you want to inspect. The example uses lab_requests. Empty tables can return no rows without an error.
Select the SQL button above the results to show the generated SELECT. Plain table browsing has no guaranteed row order.
Use the page size and arrows for larger results. Add a deliberate ORDER BY ending in a unique key before relying on stable pages.
tasks.result: The tab reads current rows from the selected connector. The screenshot warehouse has no requests.

tasks.title: Run a warehouse count
intro: Use a small read-only query to confirm the connector and the result. Your request count can differ from the picture.
steps: Select the plus labelled new query in the tab bar.
Open Connector and select the database you intend to query.
Enter SELECT COUNT(*) AS requests FROM lab_requests in the editor.
Select Run. The result has one requests column and one row, including when the count is zero.
tasks.result: The result shows the current warehouse request count.

tasks.title: Add a required date-range parameter
intro: Use parameters when the same query should ask for values each time it runs. This example counts requests from an included start date up to an excluded end date.
steps: Replace the SQL with SELECT COUNT(*) AS requests FROM lab_requests WHERE authored_at >= {{ param.from }} AND authored_at < {{ param.to }}.
Select Parameters above the SQL editor.
Open the Parameter actions dots in the sheet and choose Add.
Enter period as Variable ID. Date-range parameters supply the special from and to values used by the SQL.
Enter a clear Label, such as Period.
Turn on Required because this SQL needs both dates.
Open Parameter actions and select Save. This updates the current query tab. Save the query itself when you want to keep it.

tasks.title: Run with chosen dates
intro: Use dates matching your reporting question. The example includes 2026-01-01 and excludes 2027-01-01. That is the whole 2026 calendar year.
steps: Select Run. A Run parameters sheet asks for the configured values.
Set the first date to the included start. Set the second to the excluded end used by this SQL. Different SQL can use a different boundary rule.
Select the dots in the Run parameters sheet.
tasks.result: The result counts only requests inside the SQL date bounds. Zero is a valid count.

tasks.title: Save the custom query
intro: Save the SQL, connector and parameter definition when other work needs to reuse them.
steps: Open Query actions above the editor and select Save.
Enter a unique name. The example uses Requests in a date range.
Open Name actions in the naming sheet and choose Save.
tasks.result: The query appears under Custom Queries in the Explorer. Later saves update the same definition.

tasks.title: Rename a saved query
intro: Use Rename to keep the existing query identifier and its report links. Renaming does not save unsaved editor changes.
steps: Expand Custom Queries and use the dots beside the saved query.
Select Rename in that row menu.
Enter the new unique name, then open Name actions and choose Save. The example becomes Request count by period.
tasks.result: The Explorer shows the new name and the query retains its identifier.

tasks.title: Organise a query in a group
intro: Groups arrange this installation's Explorer. They do not change a query's SQL or report bindings.
steps: Select the dots beside Custom Queries.
Enter a useful name, then use Name actions and Save. The example uses Documentation examples.
Open the query row dots, point at Move to group and select the destination group. Expand that group to see the query.
tasks.result: The saved query appears inside its group.

tasks.title: Export selected queries
intro: Use an export to move names, SQL, parameters and group names between installations. Review the file before sharing source-specific content.
steps: Open Transfer actions in the Explorer header and select Export queries.
Tick only the queries you intend to export.
Open the export sheet dots and choose Download. Close the sheet when finished.
tasks.result: The JSON file contains the selected definitions. It omits query identifiers and connector bindings.

tasks.title: Review and import a query file
intro: Use this for an exported query file or an approved content pack. Check same-name behavior before applying it.
steps: Open Transfer actions and select Import queries.
Open the import sheet dots, choose Choose file and pick the query export.
Check whether each name is new, skipped or replaced. The example already exists, so it will be skipped with replacement off.
Check the connector and replacement choice
Choose the connector for newly imported names. Leave Replace existing queries off when you want to preserve existing definitions. Turn it on only when you intend replacement.
Open the sheet dots and select Import. One invalid definition prevents the file from being imported.
tasks.result: The reviewed operation creates, skips or replaces the names as shown. Replacement keeps an existing query identifier and connector.

tasks.title: Open a workflow dataset
intro: Use this when a workflow has already prepared the rows you need. No workflow dataset is required for the other tasks in this guide.
steps: Select its name. The example opens request_summary, created in Scheduled reports with workflows. It contains one requests value of zero.
tasks.result: The tab displays the saved workflow rows.

tasks.title: Run a saved query on a phone
intro: The Explorer starts collapsed so the workspace has more room. A large screen is easier for writing SQL.
steps: Select Expand explorer at the top of its narrow rail.
Expand Custom Queries and its group, then select the query name.
Select Collapse explorer to give the editor more width.
Select Run and fill the parameter sheet. Use Run actions and Run with these values as on desktop.

tasks.title: Remove a group and keep its queries
intro: Use this when the folder is no longer useful. Removing a group keeps every query it contains.
steps: Use the dots beside the group name.
Read the confirmation explaining that queries remain, then select Delete group.
tasks.result: The folder disappears and its queries appear outside it.

tasks.title: Remove an unneeded saved query
intro: Check report dependencies before deleting a query. This example removes a disposable definition and keeps the reviewed query.
steps: Use the dots beside the unneeded saved query.
Select Delete query. This removes the saved definition, not warehouse rows.
Read the confirmation, then choose Delete query only for the definition you intend to remove.
tasks.result: The saved definition disappears from the Explorer.

end.title: Choose parameter types
paragraphs: Text accepts a value read as {{ param.variableId }}. Select asks for one value from Options SQL. Its first returned column supplies the choices. Date range supplies {{ param.from }} and {{ param.to }}.
Choose a unique nonempty Variable ID for each parameter. The parameter row dots can move it up or down or remove it. Removing a parameter still referenced by SQL causes an unbound-parameter error.

A blank optional value becomes an empty string. SQL must explicitly handle that empty value when it means no filter. Required does not invent a default. A report uses template parameters, so match its parameter key to the saved query definition.

The current Reports page passes date filters as flat from and to values. A Custom Query declaring one daterange parameter works in this workbench but currently fails when bound directly to Reports. For reporting, use two Text query parameters named from and to, referenced by {{ param.from }} and {{ param.to }}. Report Designer can expose them through one Date range control.

end.title: Remove or regroup definitions
paragraphs: A saved query row offers Rename, Move to group and Delete query. No group moves a query back to the top-level list. Deleting a saved query requires confirmation and can break reports that reference it.

Each group has Rename group and Delete group. Deleting a group keeps its queries and moves them out. Dragging a query onto a group is another way to move it. On a phone, use Move to group for a direct menu action.

Refresh under Transfer actions reloads Explorer entries changed elsewhere, including by CLI or content pack imports. Group organisation belongs to this installation and is not sent through central-to-lab sync.

end.title: Keep paged results consistent
paragraphs: PostgreSQL and MySQL show a counted total. SQL Server can show total unknown and enables Next only when another row was found. Changing Rows per page returns to the first page.

For stable paging, finish ORDER BY with a unique key. For example, ORDER BY authored_at, id breaks equal-time ties when id is unique. Rows can still change while you page because the workbench does not hold a database snapshot.

A SQL Server connector without a Database can show accessible databases before schemas. Use full database, schema and table names for cross-database SQL on the same server. PostgreSQL connectors read one database each.

end.title: Export or import from the CLI
paragraphs: Read Start here for the launcher on your platform. Use your real installation folder, such as ~/Downloads/openldr_ce or C:\openldr_ce. A development checkout uses pnpm openldr instead of openldr.
html:
openldr query export --out data/queries.json --name "Request count by period"
openldr query import data/queries.json
Export overwrites an existing output file. Import skips existing names by default. Add --force only when you intend to replace them. Content for one lab system belongs in operator-managed pack files.

end.title: Optional practice query file
paragraphs: Download the single reviewed query export. It asks for dates and counts warehouse requests. It contains no patient rows and needs no sample bundle. Import it only if you want a reference after writing your own query.
For a practice dataset, follow the optional count workflow in Scheduled reports with workflows. Datasets can be absent on a new installation.

end.title: Troubleshooting
paragraphs: No sources are available. Ask a manager to configure an enabled database connector or create the workflow dataset you need.
A query fails. Read the error replacing the result. Correct SQL or values and run again. Old results are not a successful new answer.
An unbound parameter is reported. Match every SQL parameter to a configured definition. Date ranges use the from and to values.
A Select list is empty. Run its Options SQL in a separate tab. It may legitimately return no rows.
A name already exists. Choose another name. The naming sheet preserves the draft after a rejected duplicate name.
An imported change disappears after restart. Built-in definitions can be seeded again. Create a separate custom name when you need a durable variation.

end.title: Related guides
paragraphs: Report Designer binds saved query output to a page. Reports runs library entries. Connectors configures data sources.
